{"perspective":"process_change","title":"Check and annotate condition before completing return records","mechanism":"C1 describes return recording preceding condition inspection, with missed annotations. Reverse that order using the agreed condition-first paper checklist described in C2: inspect the item, explicitly record its condition, then complete the return record. The proposed mechanism is a completion gate that keeps condition assessment from becoming an easily skipped follow-up task. Staff retain judgment over condition; uncertain findings should be marked for review rather than treated as satisfactory. C2 supports this workaround within the simulation, not a measured real-world effect.","intended_users":"Simulated ceramics lending-desk staff who inspect returned items and complete return records.","smallest_version":"Use one paper checklist at the return desk with an item identifier, condition finding, and confirmation that the finding is recorded before return completion. Agree the sequence with desk staff: inspect, annotate, then record completion. Provide an explicit pending-review option for uncertain condition. For a locally chosen bounded batch of returns, tally completed records missing condition annotations. This is a proposed procedure, not an executed test.","measurable_outcome":"Count completed returns missing condition annotations and report that count over total returns reviewed. Aim for zero omissions in a bounded batch; baseline frequency and achieved improvement are unknown.","feasibility":"C2 explicitly states that an agreed condition-first paper checklist addresses the omission without software integration. Implementation needs paper, a shared understanding of acceptable condition annotations, and staff time to inspect before completing records. No network, deployment, personal data, or new metered spending is proposed. Only synthetic observations are available; throughput effects, adherence, and inspection consistency remain unmeasured.","maintenance":"Keep the checklist available, orient staff to the sequence, and periodically review omissions and pending cases. Revise wording if staff interpret condition categories inconsistently; ongoing effort is unknown.","software_warranted":{"verdict":"no","reason":"The supplied evidence identifies a sequencing problem and an agreed paper workaround that addresses it (C1, C2), not a missing technical capability. A process change with human condition judgment is the smallest supported response; neither a new application nor integration is justified. Existing recording tools can remain unchanged. Reconsider only if observed omissions persist despite adherence or paper handling creates a material, measured burden."},"recommendation":"recommend","claim_refs":["C1","C2"],"assumptions":[{"statement":"Staff can inspect and annotate returns before completing their records without violating another required workflow.","would_change":"If initial recording is mandatory, use a clearly pending return state and require condition annotation before final completion instead."},{"statement":"The agreed checklist is available and usable during routine desk work, as C2 suggests.","would_change":"If access or adherence fails, address placement, workload, and training before considering technical enforcement."},{"statement":"Condition findings can be expressed on paper, with uncertain cases identified for human review.","would_change":"If staff cannot assess condition reliably, add agreed criteria and qualified review; sequencing alone would not solve assessment errors."}],"novelty":null,"response_to_findings":null}
